items.title: Nvidia shares fall in premarket trading as Jensen Huang’s return sparks US political backlash – business live
items.summary:
Republicans and Democrats object over Trump’s role in Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO, following an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

  • Republican senators criticize Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang


Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, despite concerns over his conduct and the supply of AI chips to China, may show that AI – and Huang himself – are ‘too big to fail’.

That phrase was on everyone’s lips almost 20 years ago when the Global Financial Crisis struck, and several major banks were bailed out.

Given Nvidia’s pivotal role in the AI capex rollout, the implications of Huang’s reinstatement could be profound. Borrowing from the GFC, are some technology CEOs now so systemically important to the future of AI and US leadership in the latest technology revolution that they cannot be fired?

Questions around the scale of financing required and future monetisation remain, and the dependence on Huang for the future success of AI may paradoxically heighten those concerns especially given Anthropic fell despite yesterday’s broad market rally.

“We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions. Congress must come together in swift bipartisan action and demand answers immediately.”
items.t: Asia-Pacific markets rally as Huang’s return to Nvidia reignites AI trade, despite US political backlash – business live

items.title: Billionaire Frank Slootman gives 22,081 Montana kids $1,000 each for their Trump Accounts
items.summary:
Snowflake billionaire Frank Slootman and his wife, Brenda, are giving more than $22 million to children in their home state of Montana. The couple is putting $1,000 into the Trump Account of every Montana child born in 2023 or 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department announced on Nov. 19 .

The gift covers 22,081 children, totaling $22,081,000. The Slootman Family Foundation said the money has already been deposited through the Treasury Department and invested in the children’s accounts, according to NBC Montana .

Those children were born too early for the federal government’s own $1,000 deposit, which goes only to children born from 2025 through 2028. The Slootmans’ gift gives them the same start. At $1,000 a child, it is also four times the per-child amount in Michael and Susan Dell’s $6.25 billion national pledge .

“Montana is the Last Best Place,” the Slootmans said in a statement. “We want to give Montana children an even faster start in life. The money in your account is yours, it cannot be accessed by anybody, not even by you until you are at least 18 years old. What you can do is watch it grow, ask for contributions on birthdays, holidays and other special occasions to make your account compound in value even more.”

Gov. Greg Gianforte thanked the family for what he called “this significant investment.”

A Snowflake fortune with Montana roots 

Frank Slootman, Snowflake’s chairman and former CEO, led the cloud data company through its 2020 initial public offering after taking two other technology companies, Data Domain and ServiceNow , public. Bloomberg Law reported…
items.t: Billionaire Frank Slootman gives 22,081 Montana kids $1,000 each for their Trump Accounts

items.title: ‘Accountability becomes negotiable:’ 14 business leaders react to Jensen Huang’s return
items.summary:
In today’s CEO Daily: CEOs have mixed feelings about Huang’s comeback. 

The big leadership story: Gwynne Shotwell, the billionaire who really runs SpaceX, faces her next test. 

The markets: Nvidia shares fell in premarket trading after Monday’s Huang-inspired rebound. 

Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . 

Good morning —or should I say, good grief? Jensen Huang’s 11-day timeout ended yesterday as Nvidia’s board unanimously reinstated him as CEO, having last week rejected his offer to return. Investors cheered, sending the stock up 30% on the news, although S&P 500 futures already pointed to a rebound in the market. His colleagues cheered, perhaps for fiscal rather than emotional reasons amid allegations that their old boss often belittled them—and slept with a direct report. Elon Musk declared that “the mistake has been corrected” while fellow X influencer Bill Ackman wrote that “the wisdom of the crowd prevails.” And President Donald Trump took credit for the move, with a spokesman telling Fortune “we have to protect our geniuses.”

If you felt a pit in your stomach at hearing the news, you’re not alone. Even the prediction markets didn’t spot this one coming as Huang faces a plethora of probes, investigations, lawsuits, and questions over whether he compromised national security, misled investors, violated corporate policies, and more. When the scandal first broke, several leaders told me Huang had to go , even though it might trigger a selloff. Nvidia remains a cautionary tale on the perils of an unchecked CEO and an ecosystem that relies too much…
items.t: ‘Accountability becomes negotiable:’ 14 business leaders react to Jensen Huang’s return

items.title: Why Xi’s brief APEC handshake with Takaichi reflects a frozen China-Japan relationship
items.summary:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi shook hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen last week, the closest thing to a thaw in China-Japan relations since late last year.

The encounter, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting, was brief. Takaichi shook hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, as they greeted arriving guests. Yet apart from a few other brief interactions, Xi and Takaichi held no official meeting.

Observers believe that Takaichi’s brief handshake with Xi reflects a relationship now driven more by security than by trade. Complicating matters is U.S. President Donald Trump’s relationship with Beijing, which Tokyo fears may drive a wedge between Japan and its closest ally. 

Why are China and Japan at odds? 

Relations between Tokyo and Beijing deteriorated sharply in November 2025, when Takaichi told Japan’s parliament that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could prompt Japan to deploy its Self-Defense Forces if the conflict posed an existential threat.

That same month, Beijing demanded that Takaichi retract her comments, calling them “egregious.” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian warned that Japan “must bear all consequences.” He also said that if Japan intervened militarily in a Taiwan Strait conflict, China would “strike back decisively.” 

China advised its citizens to avoid traveling to Japan shortly after Takaichi’s comments in November 2025. It also imposed export restrictions on dual-use technology, including rare earth elements, permanent magnets, and other critical minerals used in defense…
items.t: Why Xi’s brief APEC handshake with Takaichi reflects a frozen China-Japan relationship

items.title: Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens to $120 million despite GTA VI—and its audience explains why
items.summary:
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to an estimated $120 million in North America this weekend, nearly three times the $44 million debut of its 2023 predecessor, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes . The Lionsgate prequel added $105 million overseas for a $225 million global launch, returning the franchise to the three-figure heights of its original run.

It did so in the shadow of Grand Theft Auto VI , the long-awaited Rockstar Games release that arrived one day earlier. Fans and industry insiders alike speculated that the game, which topped $1 billion in pre-sales ahead of its Nov. 19 launch, would monopolize the attention economy and drain an already thin November box office .

In hindsight, releasing a Hunger Games movie the day after GTA VI may have been a clever piece of counterprogramming. “I think the marketplace has already spoken,” Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian told the Associated Press.

Two franchises, two very different audiences 

Both GTA and The Hunger Games are now multigenerational action franchises, but the former has always targeted men, mostly young-adult to 40-year-old gamers drawn to its edgy depictions of criminal violence. The Hunger Games , meanwhile, has its roots in teen readers and women.

Like the five films before it, Sunrise on the Reaping is adapted from Suzanne Collins’ young-adult novels. It centers on 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, played by Joseph Zada, but the series was built around its heroine, Katniss Everdeen. Jennifer Lawrence, who led the original four films as Katniss, returns for a brief epilogue cameo.

The…
items.t: Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens to $120 million despite GTA VI—and its audience explains why

items.title: On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest
items.summary:
In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years . January’s benefits will be 3.6% higher, lifting the average retired worker’s monthly check to about $2,170, according to the Social Security Administration’s 2027 COLA announcement . The larger adjustment reflects persistent inflation in 2026.

Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first. Starting in January, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on Nov. 17 that the standard Part B premium rises by $6.50 to $209.40 a month. For most retirees, that premium is deducted straight from their Social Security benefit.

Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise. And because the premium is a flat amount, the smaller the check, the bigger the share it takes.

Smaller checks lose a bigger share of the raise 

For a retiree collecting the 2026 average of $2,095 a month, the 3.6% COLA adds about $75. After the higher premium, roughly $69 remains, so Medicare claims about 9% of the increase.

Lower down the scale, the bite grows. A $1,000 monthly benefit rises by $36, but only $29.50 survives the premium hike, an 18% haircut on the raise. At $1,500 a month, the COLA is worth $54 and the net gain is $47.50, meaning 12% of the raise goes to Medicare.

Bigger checks barely feel it. A $2,500 benefit gains $90 and keeps $83.50, losing 7% of the increase. At $3,000 a month, the raise is $108, the net gain is $101.50, and the premium takes just 6%.

That math applies to retirees who pay…
items.t: On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

items.title: Engineer, saleswoman, Elon Musk whisperer: Meet Gwynne Shotwell, the billionaire who really runs SpaceX
items.summary:
In 2002 Gwynne Shotwell had a lunch that would change her life—and the trajectory of the business world as we know it. Then 38, she had been working for a decade at a rocket startup, frustrated at the pace of innovation on the ground. “It wasn’t a vibrant industry, and we hadn’t gotten back to the moon [in 30 years],” she said on a podcast in 2022. “The systems were designed to eliminate risk, so they took forever and cost too much.” A former colleague had just departed for another rocket startup, and she met him to celebrate at a favorite Austrian restaurant in the coastal L.A. suburb of El Segundo. Afterward, her friend suggested Shotwell stop by his new company to meet the owner.

The owner, of course, was Elon Musk. Fresh off making a fortune at PayPal , Musk laid out his vision to the curious Shotwell: make rockets a lot more cheaply than NASA; sell launches to commercial satellite companies at super-bargain prices; slash prices even more by making the rockets reusable. Shotwell blurted out that he needed a “business developer,” effectively a sales leader who could win the pre-product contracts needed to fund the vision. Musk called her with an offer, and within days, Shotwell came aboard SpaceX. “I knew that working for Elon would be my last job in aerospace,” she has often said.

The investors and funds that have bought shares in SpaceX since its debut as, pre-Anthropic , the biggest IPO of all time are placing a huge bet on the visionary genius of Elon Musk. Though they may not realize it, those investors are also betting on the far lesser-known figure who’s spent…
items.t: Engineer, saleswoman, Elon Musk whisperer: Meet Gwynne Shotwell, the billionaire who really runs SpaceX

items.title: Women’s football has a $1 billion opportunity—and the WSL wants a slice of the pie
items.summary:
The 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup final was a watershed moment for the sport, with record-breaking attendance and viewership numbers. More than 40 million people in North America tuned in to watch the U.S. beat China 5–4 on penalties in the final. Among them was ­ Canadian Nikki Doucet, then a student and college basketball player at St. Francis Xavier University. “That was the first time I’d seen women’s team sports on TV, and I remember feeling so excited,” she says.

Since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly. Its global fan base is projected to surpass 800 million by 2030, according to Nielsen Sports, while Fifpro expects the sport to be a $1 billion industry by 2027—a 72% increase from 2024.

Now CEO of Women’s Super League Football, the company responsible for operating the top two English women’s leagues (WSL and WSL2), Doucet is at the sharp end of that opportunity. England has become a commercial force in women’s football: Eight of the world’s 15 highest-revenue clubs are in the WSL, according to Deloitte, and Doucet believes the league is well-positioned to capture a “significant portion” of the potential $1 billion the sport is predicted to generate.

American entrepreneurs and investment groups are taking note. The success of the WNBA—now an $850 million franchise— underlines the potential, and many see an opportunity to buy in at an early stage in the commercial development of the sport.

U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include…
items.t: Women’s football has a $1 billion opportunity—and the WSL wants a slice of the pie

items.title: Why is gas suddenly cheaper? Five factors driving the drop to $3.64 a gallon
items.summary:
The average price of gasoline in the U.S. has plunged nearly 90 cents a gallon in two months down to its lowest level since the early days of the Iran war, coming just in time for Thanksgiving travel.

Context, of course, matters. The average price for a gallon of regular unleaded was $3.64 on Monday. Though that’s 57 cents higher than the price a year ago, according to AAA, it has come down precipitously of late. And it would only hace to fall a bit further to $3.58 to hit where it stood on Thanksgiving Day 2022. Over the weekend, in some parts of the country, prices at the pump could be seen hovering at—or occasionally even below—the $3 mark, a huge psychological break for consumers who have suffered through years of rising prices. 

“The scale of decline has been a little bit surprising,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “But, given how things have developed, it’s not really a shock.”

So, why have prices fallen so sharply since late September? It’s a combination of geopolitical factors in the Middle East, typical seasonal declines, and refinery operational issues. And, no, there wasn’t any conspiracy to keep prices higher ahead of the midterm elections. However, President Donald Trump’s actions are key contributors.

Here are the five main factors causing fuel prices—especially gasoline—to tumble:

More oil exports are exiting the Middle East, including from the now-infamous Strait of Hormuz

items.t: Why is gas suddenly cheaper? Five factors driving the drop to $3.64 a gallon

items.title: TSMC gains $158 billion in value in one day as Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO
items.summary:
Asian stocks rallied on Tuesday after the board of Nvidia—the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom—voted Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership crisis that had battered the region’s AI supply chain. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), which makes Nvidia’s chips, surged 9.9%, the daily limit, adding 5.2 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($158 billion) to its market value in a single day.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 rose 3.9% as the market returned from a three-day weekend, while South Korea’s KOSPI surged 6.2% and Taiwan’s TAIEX climbed 9%.

Tuesday’s rally marks a rebound after a brutal stretch for the AI trade . The TAIEX fell by 17.5% last week, its worst such drop since 1991, pushing regulators to impose market stabilization measures, such as banning short selling, over the weekend.

Foxconn and Wistron , which assemble AI servers around Nvidia’s chips, rose almost 10%. SK Hynix, the world’s leading manufacturer of high-bandwidth memory, climbed 6.7%, while Samsung Electronics rose 6.6%. In Japan, Kioxia, Toshiba’s former memory chip unit, surged 10.0%, and Advantest, which makes chip-testing equipment, jumped 12.5%.

“This looks like a powerful relief rally, amplified by short covering and the sharp selloff that preceded it,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank, says. “The initial rebound could extend over the next few trading sessions, particularly in semiconductor-heavy markets such as Taiwan and South Korea, where earnings visibility has improved following [Jensen] Huang’s return.” 

Yet the relief from Huang’s…

items.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
items.summary:
Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes?

In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north.

That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way.

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: A selloff, a POTUS, or a recession: What really made Nvidia bring Jensen Huang back as CEO?
items.summary:
The instant the news hit the wires Monday morning that Jensen Huang was back in the job as Nvidia CEO, shares of the AI chipmaker surged 29% in premarket trading. They went on to notch their best session in more than 20 years, while the broad-market S&P 500 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq jumped about 4.7% and 6.5% respectively.

What a change from last week, when the markets flashed red for two days and closed Friday in correction territory.

The news, at least for Monday, appears to have revived the AI trade and helped erase more than a week’s worth of losses for both the equities market and the tech behemoth.

Still, as investors celebrated and President Donald Trump took credit for Huang’s return, the big question looming over the stunning sequence of events revolved around cause and effect. Were the selloff and the Monday rally both reflections of Huang’s essential role in the global economy? Or was last week’s decline the result of broader, and still unresolved, instability in the markets that conveniently armed Huang’s supporters with a rationale to bring him back?

The sudden change of mind within Nvidia’s board —insisting the former CEO had no future at the company last week, and then saying exactly the opposite on Monday—added to the questions and sense of intrigue. What led the company to change its mind so abruptly, and why now?

Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, wasn’t surprised that the selloff might have pushed the board’s hand. “There is a good reason to think that, with shareholders in play, they would think maybe, ‘We need Jensen back…
items.t: A selloff, a POTUS, or a recession: What really made Nvidia bring Jensen Huang back as CEO?

items.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
items.summary:
On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing

During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.

Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels.

items.t: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial

items.title: NHS caterer Compass ‘plans stock market switch’ in blow to London
items.summary:
The £43bn firm’s decision to move primary listing to New York would mark latest loss for FTSE 100

Compass, one of the biggest companies in the FTSE 100, is planning to switch its primary listing from London to the US in the latest blow to the struggling UK stock market.

The £43.6bn ($57bn) catering firm, which has been listed in London since 1988, could announce its intention to move its listing to New York as soon as Tuesday when it reports its annual results.

items.t: NHS caterer Compass ‘plans stock market switch’ in blow to London

items.title: Capita boss exits and shares crash after civil service pensions failures
items.summary:
Price plunges 70% as Adolfo Hernandez leaves with ‘immediate effect’ amid continued fallout from pension payment problems

The chief executive of the troubled outsourcing group Capita has abruptly departed as he admitted it has “not delivered” for retired civil servants left waiting for pension payments.

Adolfo Hernandez has agreed to step down with “immediate effect”, the company said on Monday. He is to be replaced by the chief financial officer, Pablo Andres.

Continue reading...
items.t: Capita boss exits and shares crash after civil service pensions failures

items.title: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears
items.summary:
Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves

European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills.

The Dutch month-ahead contract – the European benchmark for gas prices over the next four weeks – rose by as much as 8.6% to €96.08, before settling up 4% at €92.50.

items.t: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears

items.title: Cost of renting in Britain to rise twice as fast as buying amid shortage of properties
items.summary:
Rents to rise by 14% until at least 2029, Hamptons predicts, as high demand for properties and low supply push up costs for tenants

The cost of renting a home in Britain is expected to rise about twice as fast as that of buying one until at least 2029, according to research, with shrinking supply pushing up the prices paid by tenants.

Rents on newly agreed lets are forecast to grow by 14.2% between 2026 and 2029, compared with house price growth of 7.2%, according to forecasts from estate agent Hamptons.

Continue reading...
items.t: Cost of renting in Britain to rise twice as fast as buying amid shortage of properties

items.title: UK taxpayers held more than £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows
items.summary:
Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama, raising fears over cost to public purse

The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures.

Continue reading...
items.t: UK taxpayers held more that £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows

items.title: Cloned number plate victims in England and Wales to get new reporting tool
items.summary:
Police launch initiative after steep rise in criminals using method to evade detection and avoid paying penalties

Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned.

Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Golf did not move from outside her London home while she was on holiday in Canada, but a similar vehicle with a fraudulent copy of her registration racked up penalty notices totalling £2,560 across five London boroughs.

items.title: The looming UK winter may spawn a double headache for Andy Burnham | Richard Partington
items.summary:
‘Raising growth in every postcode’ has been the PM’s rallying cry but deep regional disparities and rising energy bills pose problems this winter

Andy Burnham faces two, related problems: Britain faces deep regional disparities and it is entering the coldest months of the year with rising inflation.

Since entering Downing Street, raising “growth in every postcode” has been the prime minister’s rallying cry, as he bids to close the gaping chasm in living standards between the richest and poorest areas of the country. But as the war in the Middle East intensifies, the task of spreading prosperity far and wide has only become more difficult.

items.t: The looming UK winter may spawn a double headache for Andy Burnham

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…
items.t: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris

items.title: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout
items.summary:
New draft text released at Cop31 summit after countries fail to agree on electrification and finance for developing world

Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the global need to phase out fossil fuels.

The co-conveners of the Cop31 UN climate summit, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday until late evening as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress.

Continue reading...
items.t: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout

items.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
items.summary:
Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

Continue reading...
items.t: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
